reducta-first-en

Translation status: English reader-locale proof. Term names and code fences follow the en pack; supporting prose may still be English.

First-match reduction: reduce via first returns the first element whose predicate holds, none for no match and empty sources.

Syntax: reduce via first from <tensor> [at [coords]] let <binder> { return <predicate> }

Category#

reduction

Related#

Examples#

radix/corpus/summa/reducta-first-en.fab (canonical · concept)#

First-match reduction: reduce via first returns the first element whose predicate holds, none for no match and empty sources.

# =============================================================================
# reduce via first — total first-match selection over a tensor or matrix
# =============================================================================
#
# What this teaches:
#   • `first` is a reduction operator beside sum, product, max, min, argmax,
#     argmin, all, any and count; the body is the predicate, exactly as for
#     count, any and all, and the result is the first element it accepts
#   • `T ∪ none` — no match and an empty source give `none`, never an error,
#     and the result is optional even over a statically non-empty source
#   • total evaluation — the predicate runs for EVERY element, the ones after
#     the first match included; selection is first-live in row-major order,
#     never an early exit ([1.0, 5.0, 3.0] over `> 2.0` picks 5.0, not 3.0)
#   • a predicate error rides the error channel and is never turned into `none`
#   • the source is a tensor or matrix, as for every reduction; `at [i, j]`
#     binds the coordinates of the element under test
#
# Common mistakes:
#   • `reduce via first` over a list — a reduction source is a tensor or
#     matrix; lists keep their methods
#   • expecting an index — the result is the element; read the coordinates
#     inside the predicate if you need them
#   • expecting early exit — the predicate still runs after the first match
#   • `step` grouping or a `coalesce` identity on the operator itself —
#     refused by name (`coalesce` on the whole expression is the ordinary
#     default for an optional value)
#
# See also: reduce, none, count, any, all
# =============================================================================

fn pick(tf32[3] xs) → f32 ∪ none {
    return reduce via first from xs let x { return x ≻ 2.0 }
}

fn pick_cell(tf32[2, 2] m) → f32 ∪ none {
    return reduce via first from m at [i, j] let x { return x ≻ 1.0 }
}

fn pick_past(tf32[4] xs, int start) → f32 ∪ none {
    return reduce via first from xs at [i] let x { return i ≻ start }
}

fn pick_empty(tf32[0] xs) → f32 ∪ none {
    return reduce via first from xs let x { return x ≻ 0.0 }
}

main {
    let tf32[3] xs ← [1.0, 5.0, 3.0] ↦ tf32[3]
    print pick(xs)
    let tf32[3] none_above ← [1.0, 0.5, 2.0] ↦ tf32[3]
    print pick(none_above)
    let tf32[0] nothing ← empty
    print pick_empty(nothing)
    let list<f32> flat ← [0.5, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]
    let tf32[2, 2] m ← flat ↦ tf32[2, 2]
    print pick_cell(m)
    let tf32[4] ys ← [10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0] ↦ tf32[4]
    print pick_past(ys, 1)
}

Expected output:

5.0
none
none
2.0
30.0
